Written in bones

By: Annalise Lubbe | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
She is a fetal osteologist and bones are her fascination. By looking at the skeleton of a newborn baby she can tell how a baby died after being abandoned by the mother.

Unique Selling Point:
By looking at a set of bones Dr Roxanne Thornton will find the doorway to the evidence that will lead her to the answers of how an abandoned baby died. And therein lies the beauty of the challenge.

In South Africa it is estimated that 3500 children are abandoned every year. 90% of them are newborn babies dumped in places such as open fields, dustbins and pit latrines. South Africa reportedly has one of the highest rates of infants being killed in the first 24 hours of their life. For every one child that survives, two die.

Our story takes us on a road of discovery: from investigating the time, manner and cause of death of the newborn, to examining and analysing the DNA evidence, and finally piecing the puzzle together by looking below the surface where the skeleton tells a personal story about our infant’s death.


Summary:
Roxanne Thornton leads a pretty normal life: She rides horses, runs her dogs, relaxes in front of the TV and takes walks in the park. Her job though, is somewhat of a mystery to most people. She describes herself as a ‘bone doctor’ who can tell how a newborn died by looking at the human remains. The answers are written in the bones she says….it contains evidence to help us find the clues to the murdered infant.

Roxanne's interest in the field was sparked when in 2012 when she was studying forensic medicine with the focus on paediatric injuries.“I went down to the autopsy room and saw a 6 month old baby wearing a little yellow baby grow and when I took it off I found she was completely sexually assaulted”, she says.

It was a long road of discovery for Roxanne. From paediatrics she took a special interest in newborn babies and bones in particular fascinated her. Today she is one of only a handful of people in the country that specialise in forensic fetal osteology. “People stay clear of it because it is distressing and because it is hard. The skeleton of a baby changes every two weeks, and you have to be able to identify it every two weeks so it is hard,” she says. Anthropologists train on adults, not on newborns. A lot of the bones look like little pebbles or they look like little segments, they don’t actually look human and that is why there aren’t alot of us doing it,” says Roxanne.

The bones of a baby are very different to that of an adult. A newborn has over 300 bones in comparison to an adult with only 200 bones. By looking at the length and fusion stage of the bones, Roxanne can tell the exact age of the infant. If the infant died of brutal force to the skull the bones will give the telltale signs.



Further information:
Roxanne is a cog in the wheel of forensic experts who assist in the recovery process. Dr Yolanda van der Heyde is a forensic pathologist. She will look at “why was the baby born dead”, if it was alive, how did it die? Was it exposure or homicide? If homicide, was it suffocated, drowned or died of blunt force trauma? Did the newborn take its first breath before it was murdered? She can tell by studying the lungs. Is there air in the lungs? If the lungs float in water, the baby was alive before being dumped.

Yolanda’s work becomes more difficult if the human remains are badly decomposed. That is when Roxanne will step in to look at the skeleton of the infant and see what the bones are telling her. Unlike with an adult, one can build a profile of the person. Was he a swimmer, what kind of body markings does he have…with a newborn baby who has only lived for minutes, seconds, there is no profile.

Dr Laura Heathfield, our forensic scientist from UCT, will examine and analyse the evidence of the crime scene to create a detailed scientific report for legal proceedings. The death of every abandoned baby who died must, by law, be investigated in the hope of finding the infant's identity. Laura will trace the evidence on the items submitted and then interpret her findings. Crucial to her work is a DNA test to build up a profile of the baby. Laura explains that a baby’s fingerprint is formed in gestation but without any match to a family member it is virtually impossible to trace the mother. But in rare cases where the police had a suspect, Laura’s work was invaluable and there was hope for a successful prosecution.

For Roxanne, every day in her lab is like building a puzzle….something she is really good at. Connecting the bones is like connecting the dots and seeing where it leads me is highly rewarding”, she says. When you ask Roxanne what is her fascination with bones, the answer is simple: “They are beautiful architecture ... .you will see.. It reminds me that there is something more out there. Roxanne hopes that through her work she can provide enough forensic evidence from the bones to help the police with their investigation. “I am driven by results and my ultimate goal is to use my research to better our forensic process and hopefully more people will become interested in this field,” she concludes.

The story:
Interviews: Dr Yolande van der Heyde, forensic pathologist; Dr Laura Heathield, forensic scientist; Dr Roxanne Thornton, fetal osteologist.

Locations:
The new Observatory Forensic Pathology Institute in Cape Town where we will film the pathologist, Dr Yoldande van der Heyde, changing into her protective gear, ready to perform the autopsy; the x-ray room where a baby doll will be used as prop to explain the autopsy and x-ray process. A forensic officer will be present which is standard procedure. A mock-up crime scene will also be filmed to demonstrate the process of ‘finding an abandoned baby’ - once again a doll will be used as prop.
The forensic scientist, A/Prof. Laura Heathfield will be filmed at UCT in the lab where the evidence is examined and analysed.
The fetal osteologist, Dr Roxanne Thornton who works in the forensic anthropology department, will be filmed at Wits university in the anatomical lab where the bones are kept. 3D scans of past cases will be used as examples of baby’s who died and the cause of death. For ethical reasons, real human bones are not permitted to be shown. We hope to get a dummy model skeleton as prop.
We will film a real live baby, to use as overlays where Roxanne, the bone doctor, explains about the intricacy of the infant’s bones and the story they can tell us.

Final Script: Written in bones
Date: 12 October 2023
Duration: 11 minutes 3 seconds

Dr Roxanne Thornton: I am obviously a complete supernerd so.…I find beauty in the bones. I think it is beautiful architecture.

1.V/O Dr Roxanne Thornton is dedicating her life to solving mysteries. (PAUSE) But she’s not a detective - at least not in the usual sense. She unravels how abandoned babies have died, from birth, to moments and months after. And the clues lie in their delicate bones.

Lourensa Eckard: But why bones?

Dr Roxanne Thornton: I don’t know how much detail you want….

Lourensa Eckard: ….you can give it if you want.

Dr Roxanne Thornton: Everything we do in our life is literally written in the bones.

Lourensa Eckard: When we talk about a newborn with a very short lifespan I would assume that there is not a lot written yet. What do you look for?

Dr Roxanne Thornton: Foetal Osteologist, Wits University: The first thing you’re going to do is, is it human, or is it an animal? Because a lot of the time they get admitted to the service as human remains unfortunately but when you open it up it is either a small bird or a small mammal…it is mistaken quite often. If you look at your central column those can appear as little pebbles or stones. The ribs and the long bones can be mistaken for vegetation.

2.V/O They’re stories often in the headlines… but mysteries rarely solved: ‘ABANDONED BABY FOUND DEAD …HEADLINES IN THE NEWSPAPER
When an abandoned newborn dies - nameless and without identity - only their physical remains can reveal how it happened. But it takes a rare skill set and extraordinary dedication to find the answer.
Specialists like the bone doctor, the pathologist, and the forensic scientist piece together the puzzle.

A/Prof Laura Heathfield: l enjoy using my knowledge to further the field so that we can find resolution and justice for people.

3.V/O And we’ve been granted a rare glimpse into the world they inhabit.

Dr Roxanne Thornton: We currently have, many of them are illegal abortions, concealment of births or still borns and the last one which is quite disturbing is suspected infanticide. So these are children after the age of 2 months all the way up to 8 or 9 months old that have suffered violent deaths.

3.V/O About 3500 children are abandoned in South Africa every year - 90% of them are newborns left in open fields, dustbins and pit latrines. Disturbingly, our country has one of the highest rates of infants killed within the first 24 hours of life - for every child that survives, two die.

Music pause

LINK: Lourensa: behind this gate are rooms full of bones but due to ethical reasons we can’t show them to you. What we can show you are models of actual infant remains.

Lourensa Eckard: So if you look at this model, how old was this infant?

Dr Roxanne Thornton: Just based on the general shape and this opening over here which is the fontanel I would estimate this is two months or less than 2 months.

Lourensa Eckard: What kind of tools do you use to determine the age of the infant?

Dr Roxanne Thornton: Generally we would take measurements of the long bone so here we have the femur and the tibia and these measurements correspond to reference standards and they give us an idea of the gestational age of the deceased individual.

MUSIC UP: Newborn baby’s feet…hands… and little body wriggling

4.V/O A newborn has over 300 bones that are constantly developing, constantly growing - some will fuse together to become 206 bones in adulthood.

Lourensa Eckard: Roxanne, so what are we looking at here?

Dr Roxanne Thornton: This is an x-ray of a neonate or neonatal decedent or individual and you can see here at the top the cervical vertebra they are unfused….so we’ve got vertebral arches over here and the centra and these remain unfused until about between 2 and 5 years old.

Lourensa Eckard: Lourensa: So the baby’s bones are constantly fusing to form the whole?

Dr Roxanne Thornton: Absolutely! A nice analogy will be a puzzle. To think about it these components are all puzzle pieces and they are coming together to form a singular unit to support the neighbouring anatomy.

5.V/O Roxanne is one of the last witnesses to an infant's final journey.
When the baby's remains are found and reported to the police, a forensic officer collects them for the state mortuary.

That’s where our story starts - with the highly skilled team examining the body for evidence of how the child died.

Dr Yolande van der Heyde: So the body would show evidence of sharp force trauma, for example a stab wound, the body may show evidence of blunt force trauma that he has been beaten with a blunt object or the body may show evidence of strangulation.

6.V/O Dr Yolande van der Heyde, senior pathologist at Cape Town’s Observatory Forensic Pathology Institute who performs the autopsy, carefully scrutinises the little body for signs that might help investigators identify its biological mother.

Pause

V/O This unit works with cases of murdered and abandoned babies, as well as those who die after being dumped.

Dr Yolande van der Heyde: Senior Pathologist - Observatory Forensic Pathology Services: It is illegal to abandon a newborn baby and this practice may be prosecuted in a court of law.

Link: The body of a newborn baby was brought in just over a week ago, for legal reasons we can’t show you the body but we can still show you what the process entails.

UPS - pushing gurney down passage

Lourensa Eckard: So I am dressed in my protective clothing, let’s see what goes on inside this room.

7. V/O We’re shown a printed x-ray of an actual case: the body of the newborn baby, still attached to its umbilical cord.

UPS - putting body bag down on x ray machine

Dr Yolande van der Heyde: As you can see this is a pre-autopsy x-ray of an abandoned newly born baby and performing a pre-autopsy x-ray is very important because it gives us an opportunity to visualise both soft tissue and bone tissue and the bone structure can then be assessed for any form of congenital abnormalities.

UPS

8.V/O X-rays sometimes reveal abnormalities, like birth defects.
PAUSE
For our purposes the team is demonstrating on a doll….PAUSE
In the autopsy room, Yolanda opens the body to retrieve the organs, performing a series of tests that can provide valuable clues.

Lourensa Eckard: How can you determine if the baby was born alive?

Dr Yolande van der Heyde: If there is air present in the lungs this would indicate that the baby took a breath, breathed and therefore lived. The lungs would also be placed in water and should there be air in the lungs the lungs would float.

9. V/O Lungs that don’t float indicate the baby died before taking its first breath.

UPS: tape recorder: “this is a body of a baby girl, there are no signs of blunt force trauma”
10.V/O Yolande will compile a detailed report on her findings.

Then the collected evidence goes to a laboratory to test for DNA traces that might help in the search for the infant’s mother or relatives.

A/Prof. Laura Heathfield: The samples that we would analyse could be anything from the swab of the inside of the cheek to a blood sample, any bones or hard tissue from the baby, a little clipping from their nail.

11.V/O Associate professor Laura Heathfield from the University of Cape Town runs a series of tests using minute DNA samples from the evidence bag.

A/Prof. Laura Heathfield: Forensic Scientist - University of Cape Town - So if there is a DNA profile that is generated from a crime scene it can be searched against the database and hope for a match to who left that sample on the scene, so there is a chance that the biological profile of the mother or father could be on the database and that could be used as an investigative lead to identify who the parents are.

12.V/O Unless they have a criminal record, with archived DNA, finding a biological parent on the national DNA database is near impossible. But it’s hoped the efforts of experts like Laura, Yolande, and Roxanne will result in more convictions for child killers.

Up music and change of scene

Lourensa Eckard: Does it not disturb you then to work on cases like that?

Dr Roxanne Thornton: It is. There is an emotional burden to it. You learn to cope. You become desensitized that doesn’t mean if I have a particular case I don’t fall into tears sometimes.

13. V/O As taxing as the job can sometimes be, Roxanne's deep fascination with bones fuels a determination to listen to the stories they tell.

Lourensa Eckard: What goes through your mind when you analyse the remains of an infant?

Roxanne: It reminds me that there is beauty in the world…. So even though these cases come from very cruel and ugly circumstances….every case that I process I feel honoured to do that…. I am giving them space….I am giving them voice….I am giving them attention.

Fade to black and fade up to the dogs in the park scene.

________________________________________________________________________

Promo 1: 21 Seconds
V/O She has an unusual fascination with the bones of infants ….her mission? To unveil the mysteries behind the deaths of abandoned babies.
Dr Roxanne Thornton: Everything we do in our life is literally written in the bones. It’s very attractive research if you want to try and identify an individual.

Promo 2: 21 Seconds
V/O She has dedicated her life to solving mysteries….. piecing together the skeletal remains of abandoned babies who died of unnatural causes.
Dr Roxanne Thornton: I find beauty in the bones. I think it is beautiful architecture.

Promo 3: 21 Seconds
V/O Abandoned babies… dumped and forgotten…yet not by this scientist, driven to unearth the truth behind their untimely deaths.
Dr Roxanne Thornton: Every case that I process I feel honoured to do that. I am giving them space, I am giving them a voice….I am giving them attention.

MUSIC UP: Newborn baby’s feet…hands… and little body wriggling 4.V/O A newborn has over 300 bones that are constantly developing, constantly growing - some will fuse together to become 206 bones in adulthood. Lourensa Eckard: Roxanne, so what are we looking at here? Dr Roxanne Thornton: This is an x-ray of a neonate or neonatal decedent or individual and you can see here at the top the cervical vertebra they are unfused….so we’ve got vertebral arches over here and the centra and these remain unfused until about between 2 and 5 years old. Lourensa Eckard: Lourensa: So the baby’s bones are constantly fusing to form the whole? Dr Roxanne Thornton: Absolutely! A nice analogy will be a puzzle. To think about it these components are all puzzle pieces and they are coming together to form a singular unit to support the neighbouring anatomy. 5.V/O Roxanne is one of the last witnesses to an infant's final journey. When the baby's remains are found and reported to the police, a forensic officer collects them for the state mortuary. That’s where our story starts - with the highly skilled team examining the body for evidence of how the child died. Dr Yolande van der Heyde: So the body would show evidence of sharp force trauma, for example a stab wound, the body may show evidence of blunt force trauma that he has been beaten with a blunt object or the body may show evidence of strangulation. 6.V/O Dr Yolande van der Heyde, senior pathologist at Cape Town’s Observatory Forensic Pathology Institute who performs the autopsy, carefully scrutinises the little body for signs that might help investigators identify its biological mother. Pause V/O This unit works with cases of murdered and abandoned babies, as well as those who die after being dumped. Dr Yolande van der Heyde: Senior Pathologist - Observatory Forensic Pathology Services: It is illegal to abandon a newborn baby and this practice may be prosecuted in a court of law. Link: The body of a newborn baby was brought in just over a week ago, for legal reasons we can’t show you the body but we can still show you what the process entails. UPS - pushing gurney down passage Lourensa Eckard: So I am dressed in my protective clothing, let’s see what goes on inside this room. 7. V/O We’re shown a printed x-ray of an actual case: the body of the newborn baby, still attached to its umbilical cord. UPS - putting body bag down on x ray machine Dr Yolande van der Heyde: As you can see this is a pre-autopsy x-ray of an abandoned newly born baby and performing a pre-autopsy x-ray is very important because it gives us an opportunity to visualise both soft tissue and bone tissue and the bone structure can then be assessed for any form of congenital abnormalities. UPS 8.V/O X-rays sometimes reveal abnormalities, like birth defects. PAUSE For our purposes the team is demonstrating on a doll….PAUSE In the autopsy room, Yolanda opens the body to retrieve the organs, performing a series of tests that can provide valuable clues. Lourensa Eckard: How can you determine if the baby was born alive? Dr Yolande van der Heyde: If there is air present in the lungs this would indicate that the baby took a breath, breathed and therefore lived. The lungs would also be placed in water and should there be air in the lungs the lungs would float. 9. V/O Lungs that don’t float indicate the baby died before taking its first breath. UPS: tape recorder: “this is a body of a baby girl, there are no signs of blunt force trauma” 10.V/O Yolande will compile a detailed report on her findings. Then the collected evidence goes to a laboratory to test for DNA traces that might help in the search for the infant’s mother or relatives. A/Prof. Laura Heathfield: The samples that we would analyse could be anything from the swab of the inside of the cheek to a blood sample, any bones or hard tissue from the baby, a little clipping from their nail. 11.V/O Associate professor Laura Heathfield from the University of Cape Town runs a series of tests using minute DNA samples from the evidence bag. A/Prof. Laura Heathfield: Forensic Scientist - University of Cape Town - So if there is a DNA profile that is generated from a crime scene it can be searched against the database and hope for a match to who left that sample on the scene, so there is a chance that the biological profile of the mother or father could be on the database and that could be used as an investigative lead to identify who the parents are. 12.V/O Unless they have a criminal record, with archived DNA, finding a biological parent on the national DNA database is near impossible. But it’s hoped the efforts of experts like Laura, Yolande, and Roxanne will result in more convictions for child killers. Up music and change of scene Lourensa Eckard: Does it not disturb you then to work on cases like that? Dr Roxanne Thornton: It is. There is an emotional burden to it. You learn to cope. You become desensitized that doesn’t mean if I have a particular case I don’t fall into tears sometimes. 13. V/O As taxing as the job can sometimes be, Roxanne's deep fascination with bones fuels a determination to listen to the stories they tell. Lourensa Eckard: What goes through your mind when you analyse the remains of an infant? Roxanne: It reminds me that there is beauty in the world…. So even though these cases come from very cruel and ugly circumstances….every case that I process I feel honoured to do that…. I am giving them space….I am giving them voice….I am giving them attention. Fade to black and fade up to the dogs in the park scene. ________________________________________________________________________ Promo 1: 21 Seconds V/O She has an unusual fascination with the bones of infants ….her mission? To unveil the mysteries behind the deaths of abandoned babies. Dr Roxanne Thornton: Everything we do in our life is literally written in the bones. It’s very attractive research if you want to try and identify an individual. Promo 2: 21 Seconds V/O She has dedicated her life to solving mysteries….. piecing together the skeletal remains of abandoned babies who died of unnatural causes. Dr Roxanne Thornton: I find beauty in the bones. I think it is beautiful architecture. Promo 3: 21 Seconds V/O Abandoned babies… dumped and forgotten…yet not by this scientist, driven to unearth the truth behind their untimely deaths. Dr Roxanne Thornton: Every case that I process I feel honoured to do that. I am giving them space, I am giving them a voice….I am giving them attention. ________________________________________________________________________________________________

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): She is a fetal osteologist and bones are her fascination. By looking at the skeleton of a newborn baby she can tell how a baby died after being abandoned by the mother.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: By looking at a set of bones Dr Roxanne Thornton will find the doorway to the evidence that will lead her to the answers of how an abandoned baby died. And therein lies the beauty of the challenge. In South Africa it is estimated that 3500 children are abandoned every year. 90% of them are newborn babies dumped in places such as open fields, dustbins and pit latrines. South Africa reportedly has one of the highest rates of infants being killed in the first 24 hours of their life. For every one child that survives, two die. Our story takes us on a road of discovery: from investigating the time, manner and cause of death of the newborn, to examining and analysing the DNA evidence, and finally piecing the puzzle together by looking below the surface where the skeleton tells a personal story about our infant’s death.
metadata.Summary: Roxanne Thornton leads a pretty normal life: She rides horses, runs her dogs, relaxes in front of the TV and takes walks in the park. Her job though, is somewhat of a mystery to most people. She describes herself as a ‘bone doctor’ who can tell how a newborn died by looking at the human remains. The answers are written in the bones she says….it contains evidence to help us find the clues to the murdered infant. Roxanne's interest in the field was sparked when in 2012 when she was studying forensic medicine with the focus on paediatric injuries.“I went down to the autopsy room and saw a 6 month old baby wearing a little yellow baby grow and when I took it off I found she was completely sexually assaulted”, she says. It was a long road of discovery for Roxanne. From paediatrics she took a special interest in newborn babies and bones in particular fascinated her. Today she is one of only a handful of people in the country that specialise in forensic fetal osteology. “People stay clear of it because it is distressing and because it is hard. The skeleton of a baby changes every two weeks, and you have to be able to identify it every two weeks so it is hard,” she says. Anthropologists train on adults, not on newborns. A lot of the bones look like little pebbles or they look like little segments, they don’t actually look human and that is why there aren’t alot of us doing it,” says Roxanne. The bones of a baby are very different to that of an adult. A newborn has over 300 bones in comparison to an adult with only 200 bones. By looking at the length and fusion stage of the bones, Roxanne can tell the exact age of the infant. If the infant died of brutal force to the skull the bones will give the telltale signs.
metadata.Further information: Roxanne is a cog in the wheel of forensic experts who assist in the recovery process. Dr Yolanda van der Heyde is a forensic pathologist. She will look at “why was the baby born dead”, if it was alive, how did it die? Was it exposure or homicide? If homicide, was it suffocated, drowned or died of blunt force trauma? Did the newborn take its first breath before it was murdered? She can tell by studying the lungs. Is there air in the lungs? If the lungs float in water, the baby was alive before being dumped. Yolanda’s work becomes more difficult if the human remains are badly decomposed. That is when Roxanne will step in to look at the skeleton of the infant and see what the bones are telling her. Unlike with an adult, one can build a profile of the person. Was he a swimmer, what kind of body markings does he have…with a newborn baby who has only lived for minutes, seconds, there is no profile. Dr Laura Heathfield, our forensic scientist from UCT, will examine and analyse the evidence of the crime scene to create a detailed scientific report for legal proceedings. The death of every abandoned baby who died must, by law, be investigated in the hope of finding the infant's identity. Laura will trace the evidence on the items submitted and then interpret her findings. Crucial to her work is a DNA test to build up a profile of the baby. Laura explains that a baby’s fingerprint is formed in gestation but without any match to a family member it is virtually impossible to trace the mother. But in rare cases where the police had a suspect, Laura’s work was invaluable and there was hope for a successful prosecution. For Roxanne, every day in her lab is like building a puzzle….something she is really good at. Connecting the bones is like connecting the dots and seeing where it leads me is highly rewarding”, she says. When you ask Roxanne what is her fascination with bones, the answer is simple: “They are beautiful architecture ... .you will see.. It reminds me that there is something more out there. Roxanne hopes that through her work she can provide enough forensic evidence from the bones to help the police with their investigation. “I am driven by results and my ultimate goal is to use my research to better our forensic process and hopefully more people will become interested in this field,” she concludes. The story: Interviews: Dr Yolande van der Heyde, forensic pathologist; Dr Laura Heathield, forensic scientist; Dr Roxanne Thornton, fetal osteologist. Locations: The new Observatory Forensic Pathology Institute in Cape Town where we will film the pathologist, Dr Yoldande van der Heyde, changing into her protective gear, ready to perform the autopsy; the x-ray room where a baby doll will be used as prop to explain the autopsy and x-ray process. A forensic officer will be present which is standard procedure. A mock-up crime scene will also be filmed to demonstrate the process of ‘finding an abandoned baby’ - once again a doll will be used as prop. The forensic scientist, A/Prof. Laura Heathfield will be filmed at UCT in the lab where the evidence is examined and analysed. The fetal osteologist, Dr Roxanne Thornton who works in the forensic anthropology department, will be filmed at Wits university in the anatomical lab where the bones are kept. 3D scans of past cases will be used as examples of baby’s who died and the cause of death. For ethical reasons, real human bones are not permitted to be shown. We hope to get a dummy model skeleton as prop. We will film a real live baby, to use as overlays where Roxanne, the bone doctor, explains about the intricacy of the infant’s bones and the story they can tell us. __________________________________________________________________________________________________
